inline.s: [Śāriputra, one who has personally realized the Dharma, without doubt or regret, — I permit such a person to preach from the high seat. Though still a common person, if he purely observes the precepts, if his mind does not cling to the doctrines of the heterodox scriptures, if he single-mindedly seeks the supreme fruit of the śramaṇa, if he does not covet offerings, if he is skillful in the definite teaching, of wide learning and vast in parable like the great ocean, and would not speak falsely even at the cost of his life, does not delight in contention, benefits himself and others, and speaks only of the pure ultimate truth — speaking thus, he also acts thus. Śāriputra, one who speaks thus — I permit him to preach the Dharma.]

Śāriputra, one who has personally realized the Dharma, who is without doubt or regret concerning the real mark of all dharmas, — I permit such persons to preach from the high seat. Though still a common person, if he purely observes the precepts, if his mind does not cling to the doctrines of the heterodox scriptures, if he single-mindedly seeks the supreme fruit of the śramaṇa, if he does not covet offerings, if he is skillful in the definite teaching, of wide learning and vast in parable like the great ocean, and would not speak falsely even at the cost of his life, does not delight in contention, benefits himself and others, and speaks only of the pure ultimate truth — speaking thus, he also acts thus. Śāriputra, one who speaks thus — I permit him to preach the Dharma.

[One who has personally realized the Dharma]“Personally” means by oneself. The Buddha Dharma is profound; only by realizing it does one know it. Hence the Buddha says: “One who has personally realized the Dharma, without doubt or regret — I permit such a person to preach from the high seat.” [Common person]Here “common person” is used in contrast to the sages. Those above the first stage of the Lesser Vehicle (the stream-enterer) and above the first ground of the Greater Vehicle bodhisattva are sages; those below who have not yet cut off delusion are common persons.

[What the Tathāgata has spoken is able to keep the various dharmas from going against one another — namely, speaking of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who seeks profit, who has left home for the Buddha and yet breaks the body of precepts — what use is his preaching! Why? Śāriputra, it is said in my scriptures: if a person is himself not good and still, and himself unable to guard himself, yet can cause others to be good, still, and self-guarding — there is no such case. It is like a person who has himself sunk in the mud and wishes to bring others out of it — there is no such case. If a person is able himself to be good and still, and able to leave the mud, and then wishes to bring others out of it — then there is such a case.]

What the Tathāgata has spoken is able to keep the various dharmas from going against one another — that is, speaking of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who seeks fame and profit, who as a disciple of the Buddha has left home yet breaks the body of precepts — how can he preach the Dharma! Why? Śāriputra, it is said in my scriptures: if a person is himself not good and not still, and against the pollution and temptation of sense objects is himself unable to guard himself, yet wishes to teach others to be good, still, and self-guarding — that is impossible. It is like a person who is himself already drowning in the mud and still wants to pull others out of the mud — that is impossible. If a person is able himself to be good and still, and able himself to leave the mud, and then wishes to pull others out of it — then it is possible.

[Good and still]Free from desire and peaceful. The Sūtra of Forty-two Sections says: “When the World-Honored One had accomplished the way, he thought thus: ‘To be free from desire and to be still — this is the most excellent.’”

[Therefore, Śāriputra, I now declare to you plainly: to slander the Tathāgata is no light offense. A bhikṣu who speaks truthfully should be permitted to preach the Dharma; for he who is not a liar, a bhikṣu who observes the precepts, is able to give the gift of Dharma. Śāriputra, preaching from the high seat, definitely cutting off doubt, is the highest matter; if one’s keeping of the precepts is impure and one clings to heterodox meanings, I do not permit him. And liars, those who value worldly pleasures, those who seek offerings, and those who delight in contention — I likewise do not permit them. I permit those who purely observe the precepts, those of upright heart, and those who penetrate the real mark of all dharmas, to preach from the high seat. Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu had better give up the precepts than, by assuming the marks of a sage and concealing the stains of guilt under the robe, secretly do many evil deeds while receiving the faithful offerings of men. Śāriputra, for the sake of trifling causes, they receive a body in hell for a long time.]

Therefore, Śāriputra, I now tell you plainly: to slander the Tathāgata is no light offense. A bhikṣu who speaks truthfully should be permitted to preach the Dharma, because he who is not a liar, a bhikṣu who observes the precepts, is able to give the gift of Dharma. Śāriputra, preaching from the high seat, with the meaning settled and cutting off beings’ doubt, is the highest matter; if one’s keeping of the precepts is impure and one clings to the heterodox scriptures, I do not permit him to preach. And liars, those who value worldly pleasures, those who seek offerings, and those who delight in contention — I likewise do not permit them to preach. I permit those who purely observe the precepts, those of upright heart, and those who penetrate the real mark of all dharmas, to preach from the high seat. Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu had better give up the precepts than, by assuming the marks of the sage and concealing the stains of guilt under the robe, secretly do many evil deeds and receive the faithful offerings of men. Śāriputra, doing thus, for the sake of trifling causes they receive a body in hell for a long time.
[Faithful offerings]The offerings made by the faithful.

blocks.text: Appendix: Encouraging the Assembly at the Seven-Day Vigorous Practice

inline.s: Master Xingce, the Tenth Patriarch of the Pure Land School

The seven days of invoking the Name are precious above all for a single-minded, undistracted mind, without break and without mixture — it is not necessarily by rapid recitation and much recitation that one excels. One should only invoke neither too slowly nor too hastily, densely and steadily holding the Name, so that the Buddha-name in the mind stands out clearly, mark after mark. In dressing and eating, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying, the one line of the Name is continuous and unbroken, like breath itself — neither scattered nor sunk away. To invoke the Name in this way may be called one who is truly able to be single-minded and diligent in practice.
If one is a true follower of the way
(a follower of the way, one of the stream of those who study the way)
, who is able directly to investigate and realize that all dharmas are thus
(“thus” — together with dharma-nature and reality, all alternate names for the real mark of all dharmas)
, without two marks. What is meant by the “beings”
(sentient beings)
and Buddha are not two; self and other are not two; the adornment and the body are not two; the pure and the impure are not two; suffering and joy are not two; the longing
(same as 欣, joyful longing)
and revulsion are not two; grasping and letting go are not two; bodhi and the defilements are not two; birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are not two. These pairs of dharmas

(the pairs just spoken of — beings and Buddha, self and other, adornment and body, pure and impure, suffering and joy, longing and revulsion, grasping and letting go, bodhi and defilements, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa)
are all of one mark, one path, pure and undifferentiated, without the need to force them into arrangement
(to arrange, to set in order)

; one need only investigate them as they truly are. When investigation reaches its utmost, it suddenly meets with one’s own original mind. Then one knows that putting on clothes and eating rice are always samādhi; laughter and jesting, anger and scolding, are none other than the Buddha’s work; and the single-minded mind and the scattered mind in the end become idle talk. Throughout the twenty-four hours one cannot glimpse so much as a hair’s-breadth of a different mark. Even though one single-mindedly invokes
(same as 称, to name or invoke)

the name, it is the same as speaking abuse at will; and although one diligently cultivates and practices, it too is ascetic striving in a dream. Only when one has understood it thus is one a true student of the way, single-mindedly and diligently invoking the name.

[Adornment and body]The dependent retribution and the primary retribution. The lands, houses, and implements of the world, being that which the body relies upon, are called the “dependent retribution”; the body of the five aggregates temporarily compounded, being the result brought about by one’s past karma, is called the “primary retribution.”
The first single-mindedness
(the single-mindedness of invoking the Name, undistracted)
seems difficult but is easy; the latter single-mindedness
(the union with one’s own original mind)

seems easy but is difficult. But one who can achieve the former single-mindedness is certain to be reborn [in the Pure Land]; one who also achieves the latter single-mindedness may ascend to the highest grade. However, these two kinds of single-mindedness are both matters on the side of the common person on the broad earth; anyone who has a mind may cultivate and learn them. The monks and laypeople gathered in the same hall
(monastics and laypeople)

should by no means excessively exalt the sage’s state and contentedly remain in a lowly one. Each must diligently urge on his body and mind: in the near term, within seven days; in the far term, within a whole life, always holding this faith and always practicing this conduct. Even if one does not attain and realize
(even if one fails to realize this state)
the cause is nonetheless strong, and the grade of rebirth in the lotus palace
(the grade of the spiritually born within the lotus bud)
will certainly not be low. But if after the seven days one turns a deaf ear, and the familiar place
(referring to emotional attachments)
is never born, while the place of birth
(referring to the recitation of Buddha)

remains hard to ripen — ignorance and karmic habits pulling and intertwining, and one merely hopes to claim merit from the seven days while during those seven days one has never reached the ground of single-mindedness, undistracted. This is precisely what is called having little wholesome root, merit, and karmic conditions; how can one hope to be reborn in that land? As a result the Buddha’s golden-mouth sincere words come to be suspected of falsehood — whose fault is that? May all of you who have kept the seven days take heed each for yourselves and be admonished.

[Matters on the side of the common person on the broad earth]Matters on the side of the common person on the broad earth. The common person on the broad earth, also called the ordinary person of the thin earth, refers to the stage of the common person. [Thin earth]“Thin” means pressed upon. The “thin earth” is the state of being pressed upon by all the various sufferings — it refers to the realm of the common person. The Contemplation of the Pure Mind and Precepts says: “The common person of the thin earth has a stinking and mean body, and his retribution is lowly.”
(The above is taken from Master Xingce’s Pure Land Warnings.)
